submission.natural_language_explanation: The pole fires on the connective of a real-world locative phrase: a spatial preposition ('of', 'in', 'at', 'on', 'from', 'to', 'along', 'through', 'across', 'near', 'between', 'by', 'off', 'into') or a locator/copula ('located', 'situated', 'lies', 'lives', 'born', 'moved', 'headed', 'based', 'runs', 'travels', 'is') that gives the location of something in the physical world - a settlement or areal place (village, town, hamlet, suburb, capital, area, neighbourhood), a landscape feature (hill, valley, mountain, lake, river, coast, island, peninsula, harbour, road, highway), a direction (north, south, rural), a place name, or a building, business, vehicle or facility being located (house, shop, factory, church, cafe, office, airport, mine, bus, company). It is near zero where the same words are non-spatial or attach to non-geographic referents: partitive 'of' (the concept of X, the sum of X, the handle of the door, one of the teachers, because of the war), non-locative 'in' (interested in history, in order to), the position of small objects or rooms (keys in a drawer, book on the shelf, table in the kitchen, cat on the mat), abstract directions ('north of normal', 'went south'), and scientific or everyday non-geographic text. The peak is fixed by the words already read; the promoted vocabulary (towns, cities, suburbs, districts, hills, southeast, outskirts) is the geography register the pole is part of.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
On the maintenance of old codebases

Every long-lived codebase develops a folklore that never appears in the documentation. The rules are passed on by habit rather than by instruction, and they are usually negative: do not touch the scheduler, do not rename the event table, do not trust the cache in the payment path. Newcomers learn them by breaking them, and the scars are preserved in comments that read like epitaphs. The comments are, in their way, the most honest part of the system, because they were written by people who had just been surprised.

I spent four years working on one such system. It began as a small tool for a single team and grew, over a decade, into something that half the company depended on and nobody fully understood. The original author had left long before I arrived, and the only remaining trace of his thinking was a design note of three pages that argued, patiently, for a particular way of handling failure. The argument was sound when it was written. By the time I read it, three of its premises had quietly become false, and the code had been adjusted around them in ways that made the original reasoning look naive.

What interested me was not the decay itself but the way the team explained it. In order to justify each patch, someone had to construct a story about why the previous design was wrong. The stories were rarely accurate and almost never malicious. They were the natural product of people who needed a reason to change something and found one in the most recent incident. Within a year the team had a second folklore, layered on top of the first, and the two were often contradictory.

The architecture itself was not especially complicated. The parser sat in one directory, the scheduler in another, and the boundary between them was defined by a handful of functions that had once been elegant and were now grotesque. Whenever a bug appeared, the investigation went through the same sequence: read the logs, reproduce the failure, add a test, and then argue about where the fix belonged. The argument was always the same argument, and it was never really about the code.

I came to think of maintenance as a kind of translation. You take a requirement expressed in the language of the business, with all its ambiguity and impatience, and you render it into something a machine can execute. Every translation loses something, and every loss has to be paid for later. The debt is not visible in any accounting system, which is why managers find it so easy to ignore and engineers find it so hard to explain.

The best engineer I worked with had a rule for this. He said that a system should be understandable from its tests, and that if the tests could not explain the behaviour, the behaviour was not worth preserving. He was not a sentimental man, and he deleted more code than he wrote. But his systems outlived everyone else's, and the people who inherited them spoke of him with something close to gratitude. He retired before I did, and I never visited him. I meant to.

[end]

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
Notes toward a memoir (fragment, undated)

My mother kept a ledger of every debt and favour the family ever owed or was owed, written in a hand that grew smaller as the years passed and the columns lengthened. She believed that obligation was a kind of weather, something one could predict and prepare for but never argue with. The ledger began with a loan of forty pounds from her uncle, advanced without interest and repaid, according to her own annotation, 'in full, though not on time.' After that the entries multiplied: a neighbour's help with a roof, a cousin's silence during an argument, a doctor's refusal to send a bill, a teacher's recommendation that opened a door nobody in our family had known existed.

The habit of bookkeeping outlasted the debts themselves. By the time I was old enough to read the ledger, most of the people named in it were dead, and the sums had stopped meaning anything measurable. What remained was the pattern: a record of who had been kind and when, and a private accounting of what she believed we owed in return. She never spoke of it as charity, and she would not have tolerated the word. It was a set of transactions, she said, and transactions can be settled. She applied the same reasoning to apologies, to promises, and to the long silences that followed her brothers' quarrels, which she recorded in the margins with a tiny cross and a date.

I thought about that ledger many years later, when my own accounts had grown complicated in ways she would have recognised and disapproved of. I had taken a job I did not want, in order to pay for a flat I did not need, and I was spending my evenings explaining to strangers why the work mattered. The explanations were not lies exactly. They were the kind of truth that gets truer the more often it is repeated, and by the autumn I had stopped noticing the difference.

It was around then that I began walking out to the old house on Sundays. The house where she was born still stands on the edge of the village, its gable end facing the green, and the orchard behind it runs down to the stream. Nobody in the family had lived there for thirty years, but my aunt still kept a spare set of keys, and she never asked what I did with them. I would let myself in, open the shutters, and sit for an hour or two on the stairs, listening to the house settle and the swallows argue under the eaves.

The house is empty again now. My aunt sold it the year after the funeral, and the new owners repainted the shutters a colour my mother would have called vulgar. I do not miss it as much as I expected to. What I miss is the habit of going there, the hour on the stairs, and the sense, which I have never managed to recover, that the ledger could still be balanced. I have started a ledger of my own, though it is not the same thing. Mine lists appointments and payments and the names of people I mean to call; it has no margins, no crosses, and no weather in it.

[end of fragment]

explanation_scores.explanation: The pole fires on the connective of a real-world locative phrase: a spatial preposition ('of', 'in', 'at', 'on', 'from', 'to', 'along', 'through', 'across', 'near', 'between', 'by', 'off', 'into') or a locator/copula ('located', 'situated', 'lies', 'lives', 'born', 'moved', 'headed', 'based', 'runs', 'travels', 'is') that gives the location of something in the physical world - a settlement or areal place (village, town, hamlet, suburb, capital, area, neighbourhood), a landscape feature (hill, valley, mountain, lake, river, coast, island, peninsula, harbour, road, highway), a direction (north, south, rural), a place name, or a building, business, vehicle or facility being located (house, shop, factory, church, cafe, office, airport, mine, bus, company). It is near zero where the same words are non-spatial or attach to non-geographic referents: partitive 'of' (the concept of X, the sum of X, the handle of the door, one of the teachers, because of the war), non-locative 'in' (interested in history, in order to), the position of small objects or rooms (keys in a drawer, book on the shelf, table in the kitchen, cat on the mat), abstract directions ('north of normal', 'went south'), and scientific or everyday non-geographic text. The peak is fixed by the words already read; the promoted vocabulary (towns, cities, suburbs, districts, hills, southeast, outskirts) is the geography register the pole is part of.
